items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-09-04
items.q: he was trying to get up a band with Mutt Carey and all

ctx.x: Yeah. So Bill would go down to see Jelly when he moved out there. He was already sick and could hardly play. And Bill would start to get Jelly talking. He'd prod him with things like he'd say, well you're alright but you can't play the stuff like Teddy Wilson. Teddy Wilson, I know you're good for that old time stuff but you can't play that new stuff you can't get around on the piano. Or like Art Tatum and all that. So once it got Jelly so burned up that Jelly said I'll play something those guys can't play and…

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1976-02-16
items.q: they had Ori's band to come up from California with Mud Carry

ctx.x: The reason I got into the business at all was partly due to these first records I mentioned, the Jazzmen, that were so badly recorded on the little machine. About a $200 list price machine it was, a federal recorder. Some kid that worked, he was a teenage kid, I guess, that worked for Grunewald's. Happened to have it. He's the only one we could find that had any blanks around that would be able to record the band in 1942 when Dave issued the records. And those records were so bad that I'll tell you one story that…

He hadn't thrown them out fortunately, but he probably would have very soon if Dave hadn't gotten back. He could have thrown them in a wastebasket. So he thought it was just a joke, you know, that he sent something to amuse him. So Dave said, no, that's the real thing. It had to be worked on and issued. So anyway, I decided after that that I couldn't do much worse. So I got a machine. My machine only cost about $40. My brother put a little secondhand machine together and then bought an amplifier. My brother was a…
This is the fourth, okay, I got the fourth reel on.

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1975-02-02
items.q: Mutt was one of my favorite musicians and the favorite people, a great guy and a great musician, too.

ctx.x: Well, of course, we'll never know what Joe Oliver really sounded like.

No, that's right. On the records, you can't tell how big his tone was. But from all the evidence, about 100% of it, you might say, of anybody that ever talked about him in the old days that heard him, talk about the big tone. That he was almost like, say, a second Bolden after Bolden, that he had that big tone. Which would have undoubtedly been bigger than Louie. However, Joe did use a lot of these freak effects, not only hats and maybe plungers and all—not so much plungers. He had this little con mute, a little…
What about— Well, anyway, I guess if there's anything else to talk about.

items.title: Betty Lee Hanson, Joe James, George Lewis, Joe Lewis, Joe Butler, Kid Thomas Valentine, Bill Russell, Allan…
items.q: I know it was either Ori or Bud Scott. I don't remember which one. It could have been Mutt Carey.

ctx.x: Well, how important was the religious feeling in influencing all of this? Well, I think that's difficult to say, too.

Of course, for people like me that came down here years after it started, I would never know. But other people like, say, Kid Ori, for instance, and some of the first people I met in California, like Bud Scott, one of the old-timers, quite a few of those said that a lot of the music came right out of the churches of the jazz bands as if... I know it was either Ori or Bud Scott. I don't remember which one. It could have been Mutt Carey. I'm talking about Buddy Bolden. They said, well, he got all of his music right…
What about the street marches, the funeral marches? Are they all the same thing?
